flags: Suspected errors, copied unchanged: (1) foot: “Pedes lavēmus.” needs pedēs (acc. pl. -ēs; entry-294 has “Pedēs tibi oleō ungam.”). (2) sit-cross-legged: “crūribus dēcussātīs” – Lewis & Short has dĕcusso (short e, from decussis) and M-O decussâtis, so decussātīs. (3) sting-insect: Cic. Tusc. 2.52 “apis aculeum” lacks the ū of acūleum. (4) rub-in: “infricāre” lacks the long ī that entry-300 itself gives in- before f (M-O prints infricare unmarked). (5) entry-4’s pointer “infūsum”, kept only as related links, lacks the ī of īnfūsum. (6) snore: “Audīn’?” has a typographic apostrophe; burp has the house ASCII pergin'.

herbal-tea note: entry-300 says īnfūsum has long ī “as in L&S īnfundō, īnfūsus”, but Lewis & Short prints in-fundo, in-fūsus with the prefix unmarked; the note gives only the rule that in- is long before f.
pharmacy: Greek φαρμακοπωλεῖον would give pharmacopōlīum, as νοσοκομεῖον gives nosocomīum here and as urbs entry-432 writes oenopōlīum; worth checking against M-O.

No note written where the card gives no reasoning: eyelid leaves palpebra unmarked against Lewis & Short palpē^bra (common) and M-O palpêbra; cold-illness has dēstīllātiō with long ī on the strength of the card’s Bennett link (Lewis & Short dēstillātĭo, unmarked).

fever: “of his little daughter Attica” (Cic. Att. 12.1.2) means Atticus’s daughter; the English is kept as written. nettle: the card sends Catullus’s cure ōtiōque et urtīcā (44.15) to the cold record, which quotes only 44.13–14.

Periods I could not settle from the cards: phrases cited only to Traupman or M-O and not found in Lewis & Short are modern (morbō corripī, ā capite labōrāre, unguis pedis, unguēs resecāre, ē lectulō extrahere, dextram jungere cum aliquō, praeceps saliō / dēsiliō, tolūtim currere / cursitāre, which ludi entry-527 gives as Traupman 84); uncited ones are ours (in umerīs portāre / vehī, ōs contrahere, follis īnflātus; vēsīca and vēsīca īnflāta for a balloon by the card’s own words). cernuō “do a somersault” is modern (Lewis & Short: fall headlong, ante- and post-classical). nosocoma is modern (M-O: Grosse 1846) although the card says late Latin; chamomilla late (Plin. Val.); linīmentum and corȳza late as the card says, though Palladius and Caelius Aurelianus would be post-classical by converting.md; aurium dolor renaissance (M-O: Mattioli 1571); scaeva and antiae post-classical (Digest, Apuleius); Salvē! after a sneeze classical by Lewis & Short s.v. salveo (Petr. 98.4).

Folded in as alternatives with narrower glosses rather than separate records: jump down / out / across (jump); breathe in / out (breathe); big toe (toe); trot, jog (run); swim across (swim); feel sick, car sickness (nausea); decoction, linden-blossom tea (herbal tea); be ill, fall ill (ill); run a fever, a slight temperature (fever); stay awake all night (be awake); cut someone’s hair, tōnsūra (get a haircut); massage therapist (masseur); ride on someone’s shoulders (carry on one’s shoulders); be cold, coldness (feel cold). The reviewer may prefer some as records of their own.

Added Lewis & Short links, in the cards’ format, where a record’s word had none on its card: collum (neck), manus (hand), contraho (pucker), lentus (slowly), celer (quickly), oleum (oil), quiesco (rest). English supplied where the card gave none: “have a fever” for febrim habēre.

Likely overlaps with other categories (records created anyway): swim with natura entry-209 (natō) and the existing swimming record; doctor, dentist, nurse, hospital, pharmacy, chemist, doctor’s surgery with urbs entries 540, 542 and 432; barber, barbershop, get a haircut with urbs entry-543; herbal tea (īnfūsum) with culina entry-249; crush (conterō) with culina entry-124; squeeze out with culina entry-125; honey with culina entry-82; hurry (Festīnā lentē) with culina entry-298; toothpick with culina entry-416; make the bed with domus entry-419; shampoo with domus entry-64; toilet paper with domus entry-68; smear on (illinō) with domus entry-65; toenail with domus entry-66; mint, thyme, sage with natura entry-212; linden with natura entry-201; sting, mosquito with natura entry-511; louse with natura entry-512; oil with natura entry-211; feel cold with natura entries 277 and 502; jump with ludi entry-188 and sermo entries 93 and 287; massage with sermo entry-241 (rub your back); stand on tiptoe with sermo entry-283; rest with sermo entry-29; sleepy with sermo entry-56; tired with sermo entry-290; arm with sermo entry-94; run (jog) with ludi entry-527; write with computatra entry-48 (scrībō).
Domain: tamp and cram (rammed earth) belong with aedificatio, and write (scrībō, an aside on the scratch card) with writing or school; kept in corpus as the card’s category.

Elsewhere: urbs entry-542 says Traupman has no word for dentist, but Traupman lists medicus dentārius (pp. 63, 302). entry-307’s source line gives Traupman p. 350; the nightmare entry is on p. 351, which the record cites. entry-301’s otherwise unexplained p. 305 is Traupman’s vocabulary entry for doctor, so it went to doctor.
No card in this batch covers hiccup, burp or tickle, so they are not extended; the tool rewires hiccup’s related entry-300 to herbal-tea, and swimming’s and diving-board’s entry-291 to swimming-pool.

terms.comment: With the genitive of the herb: īnfūsum chamaemēlī, īnfūsum mentae (M-O cites 19th-century pharmacy Latin, e.g. infūsum flōrum chamomillae). A Neo-Latin noun from īnfundō, īnfundere, īnfūdī, īnfūsum, pour in. M-O’s distinction: an infusion is boiling water poured over the herb and left to stand; a decoction is boiled with the herb in it. Traupman has no herb tea; he gives only thea.
